name: Fixed lingual retainer

lead: A fixed lingual retainer is a small wire bonded behind the front teeth, usually the lower ones, to keep them from shifting after braces.
It works continuously without the patient having to remember to wear it, but cleaning around it is harder. Trials have compared materials and fixed versus removable designs.

paras: The wire holds adjacent teeth together so they cannot drift back toward their old positions.
Plaque and gum inflammation if not cleaned well, and the bond can fail, which is why bonding techniques have been studied.

lead: A fixed lingual retainer is a thin wire bonded to the tongue-side surfaces of the front teeth, most often the lower front teeth, to hold them in position after orthodontic treatment. It is typically bonded to the six front teeth or only the canines, and is used where relapse is considered more likely, such as after correction of severe rotations or gaps.[1]

Because it is not removed, it needs little patient cooperation, but it is harder to clean around than removable retainers.[1] Published work has compared fixed and removable retainers on microbial levels and gum health, tested different wire materials, and examined bond failure.[2][3][4][5]
infobox: Tongue-side of front teeth, usually lower
Multistrand stainless steel, fiber-reinforced composite, CAD/CAM titanium, 3D-printed resins
Fixed in place; duration set by orthodontist
Oral hygiene around wire; periodic checks for debonding

paras: Conventional versions use multistrand stainless steel wire bonded with composite. Alternatives studied include fiber-reinforced composite, CAD/CAM titanium retainers and 3D-printed nanoceramic resin retainers.[3][4][6] Laboratory work has also examined corrosion resistance of different fixed retention appliances.[7]

Fixed retainers are described as the best-performing retainer type for holding the lower incisors.[1] A study of 22 non-extraction cases reported on long-term stability after prolonged retention with a mandibular fixed lingual retainer, averaging 8.4 years.[8] A trial compared the number of bite contacts over one year in patients given wraparound Hawley retainers or maxillary Jensen plates with mandibular fixed retainers.[2] Surgical release of gum fibers (fiberotomy) and its effect on one-year rotational relapse has also been studied.[9]

Poorly cleaned retainers, fixed or removable, can lead to plaque, cavities and gum inflammation.[1] A randomized comparison of 45 patients assigned to fixed, vacuum-formed or Hawley retainers examined salivary microbial levels and periodontal status.[10] A cross-sectional study asked patients up to ten years after treatment about oral hygiene, periodontal health and satisfaction with retention.[11] Bond failure rate has been examined in relation to the primer used.[5]

Randomized trials have compared fiber-reinforced composite with multistrand steel wire in 60 patients for bleeding index and pocket depth, titanium CAD/CAM with conventional steel retainers, and fixed versus removable retainers in 45 patients.[3][10][4] Other studies include a long-term case series, a one-year bite-contact study and a cross-sectional patient-reported survey.[8][2][11]
